clue.text: It serves food boy’s first cutting on plate so badly

blocks.note: the letters to be jumbled
the opening letter of boy

explanation.surface: A waiter blames a clumsy boy for hacking at the food on a plate.
explanation.walkthrough: Jumble ON PLATE SO into TALESPOON, then cut B in after TA to get TABLESPOON.
explanation.definitionFit: A tablespoon is a large spoon used for dishing up portions at the table, so it literally serves meals.

clue.text: One of the letters repeatedly needed by tenant for rent

blocks.note: tenant uses two letters more than once; this is the first of them
one of two things is this one or that one, so the choice word sits between the two letters
the other letter tenant repeats

explanation.surface: A landlord's letter to a tenant keeps demanding the rent.
explanation.walkthrough: Tenant repeats T and N; 'one of' them is T OR N, written straight as one word. Rent here is the past participle of rend, not money for a flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Rent is the old past participle of rend, meaning ripped apart, exactly as torn is.

clue.text: Took care of offspring a tabby’s abandoned

indicators.note: letters abandoned are let loose to run wild

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone looked after a cat's kittens after the mother cat walked out on them.
explanation.walkthrough: The tabby's kittens are a red herring: the offspring are a person's children.
explanation.definitionFit: To babysit is to mind somebody's young children while the parents are away; took care of is its past tense.

clue.text: Men agree on cut in exchange for incentive

indicators.note: letters that are exchanged swap places with one another, so the phrase before it gets rearranged

blocks.note: thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Workers accept a pay cut in return for a bonus scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a wage deal; 'in exchange for' splits into the anagram signal and a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An incentive is something that spurs a person on, the same idea as a boost or spur to act.

clue.text: Fine, for example, having press against covering part of UK

indicators.note: one piece covering another wraps around it

blocks.note: to press against something is to push it
Northern Ireland, standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A newspaper campaign sounds fine, with the press pushing against a region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like an adjective meaning OK; with 'for example' it is the verb, one way to penalise. NI is Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Fining someone is one kind of penalty, so a fine is an example of how to discipline an offender.

clue.text: Spectator as weekly publication

blocks.note: someone who watches
a British newspaper that comes out on Sundays

explanation.surface: The Spectator is described as a weekly magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spectator really is a British weekly magazine, so the surface points there; but the answer is the Observer, a Sunday newspaper, and a spectator is simply a watcher.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectator is a person who watches events, and The Observer is a British paper printed once each week.

clue.text: A large number of Romans aim to get better

blocks.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
an aim or goal, as in 'the end justifies the means'

explanation.surface: Many ancient Romans hoped to improve themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A large number of Romans' reads as a crowd, but it is one Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: To mend is to heal or recover, as when a broken bone slowly repairs itself.

clue.text: I had to enter competition, it’s clear

blocks.note: a sporting contest
I'd, the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Someone concludes it was obvious they had to sign up for a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: I had shortens to I'd, which goes inside EVENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Evident means plain to see or obvious, which is one sense of clear.

clue.text: Fragrant flower daughter grew under a screen

indicators.note: in a down entry, the piece written under another follows it

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
a mask screens the face
rose, past tense of rise

explanation.surface: A daughter's scented flower grew behind a garden screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' and 'grew' push towards gardening, and ROSE is indeed the grew part, placed under D A MASK in the down grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The damask rose is an old, strongly scented rose variety grown for attar and perfume.

clue.text: Bridges are burnt once you’ve crossed this river

definitions.text: Bridges are burnt once you’ve crossed this river

blocks.note: reads as ordinary bridges set on fire behind an army
the river whose crossing by Caesar in 49 BC became the phrase for a step with no way back

explanation.surface: An army torches its bridges after fording a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Burning your bridges and crossing the Rubicon are both idioms for a point of no return; Caesar crossed this Italian river with his army and started a civil war.
explanation.definitionFit: Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, an irrevocable act, so the stream now names any decisive commitment.

clue.text: Small amount I invested in total for arena

indicators.note: money invested in a fund goes into it

blocks.note: the sum of figures is their total
a little bit
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A modest sum was put into a fund to build a sports ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested' in the surface is financial, fitting 'small amount' and 'total'; in the wordplay it simply means put inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a large venue for sport or shows, as a stadium is.

clue.text: Official authorising unusually direct note in suit

blocks.note: a lawsuit is a legal action
the letters to rearrange
one of the musical notes A to G

explanation.surface: A bureaucrat oddly approves direct placement of a note in a legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' is a lawsuit, not clothing or cards. 'Official' is an adjective here, not a person, and 'authorising' a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Accreditation is formal approval by a recognised body, the act of officially authorising someone or something.

clue.text: Activity in court to suppress fraudulent operations

blocks.note: to crush or put down
a racket is a dishonest money-making scheme

explanation.surface: A court case aims to shut down scams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, but it is a squash court. Squash rackets is the formal name of the game of squash.
explanation.definitionFit: Squash rackets is a sport played on an enclosed indoor court, the full formal name of squash.

clue.text: Within reason, is subsequently as feeble

indicators.note: subsequently means afterwards, so the second part follows the first

blocks.note: the reason for something is the why
used as it stands, inside the first WHY
the same word is used a second time
used as it stands, inside the second WHY

explanation.surface: Someone argues that a thing, within reason, later becomes weak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reason' is used twice: W(IS)HY, then W(AS)HY, the second tied on by 'subsequently'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wishy-washy describes something weak, insipid or lacking in resolve, just as feeble does.

clue.text: Popular answer in test for holder of post, initially

blocks.note: fashionable, in vogue
to try something is to test it
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A candidate hopes to get a well-liked answer into a job exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' looks like a first-letter instruction but belongs to the definition: incoming mail lands in the in-tray first.
explanation.definitionFit: An in-tray is a desk tray where incoming letters sit before being dealt with, the first stop for mail.

clue.text: One who chooses Spanish or French article, in part

blocks.note: a sector is a part of something
el is Spanish for the; French le works equally well

explanation.surface: A person picks between Spanish or French, in part.
explanation.walkthrough: Either article fits: S+EL+ECTOR or SE+LE+CTOR give the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A selector is a person who picks members of a team, a chooser.

clue.text: Standard cut in theatre, in a manner of speaking

blocks.note: par is the standard or normal level
a surgeon lances in an operating theatre

explanation.surface: A routine cut in a stage show, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre is the operating theatre, where a surgeon lances, not a stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Parlance is a particular way of using words, an idiom or jargon, as in 'legal parlance'.

clue.text: Poet’s written about English doctor

blocks.note: A. E. Housman, author of A Shropshire Lad
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A poet has composed verse about an English physician.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is A. E. Housman; E goes inside his name. 'Written about' reads as a subject, but here it means around.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a houseman was a junior hospital doctor in the first year after qualifying.

clue.text: Fabulous creature in tunic, worn unopened in each case

indicators.note: each word loses its opening letter, so neither is opened

blocks.note: tunic without its first letter
worn without its first letter

explanation.surface: A mythical beast wears a tunic still in its wrapping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unopened' sounds like a parcel; it strips the first letter from both tunic and worn.
explanation.definitionFit: The unicorn is a mythical horse with a single horn, a creature of fable.

clue.text: Inconclusive debate, event not on track

indicators.note: without a conclusion the word lacks its ending, so its last letter goes

blocks.note: a verb for debate, with its final S dropped

explanation.surface: An argument that went nowhere, a sidetracked occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: To debate is to discuss; lose the last S. 'Not on track' means a field event rather than a running race.
explanation.definitionFit: The discus throw is an athletics field event, held away from the running lanes.

clue.text: Derisive noise from audience upset performance in ring

blocks.note: a turn on stage
to ring someone is to call them on the phone

explanation.surface: A circus crowd jeers at a botched turn in the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring looks like a circus ring, but it is a phone ring. Upset in a down clue could hint at reversal, but that gives TCA; here it jumbles.
explanation.definitionFit: A catcall is a shrill whistle or jeer from a crowd showing disapproval.

clue.text: Small steps for intervening distances

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as on clothing labels
a pace is a single step

explanation.surface: Taking short strides to cover the gaps between places.
explanation.walkthrough: Small steps look like one idea, but split into S and PACES.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaces are gaps or intervals between things, the room lying between two points.

clue.text: It’s more trouble than it’s worth, chess player found before big game

definitions.text: It’s more trouble than it’s worth

indicators.note: one piece found before another comes first

blocks.note: one of the two sides in chess
big game are large wild animals hunted for sport

explanation.surface: A chess player complains a match is not worth the bother, before a big match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big game' reads as a major match, but it means large hunted animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A white elephant is a costly possession whose upkeep outweighs its usefulness, a burden disguised as a gift.

clue.text: Brave editor stood up, finally, being extremely selective

indicators.note: in a down entry, standing up means reading from the bottom

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
first and last letters of finally

explanation.surface: A courageous editor finally stood up and got choosy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' looks like a last-letter instruction, but it is the fodder whose ends are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: To brave something is to face it boldly in open resistance, the verb sense rather than the adjective.

clue.text: Others misspelled name in contract

indicators.note: a misspelled word has its letters in the wrong order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Other people got a name wrong in a legal agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a noun for a legal document, but it is the verb, to become smaller.
explanation.definitionFit: To contract is to become smaller or reduce in length, the verb sense rather than an agreement.

clue.text: Tricky part of course from which I can exit

indicators.note: the letters come from within the words that follow, taken straight out of them

blocks.note: runs from the end of which through to the first letter of exit

explanation.surface: A driver describes a hard section of a racetrack that they can get out of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky part of course' reads as a whole-clue description, and 'I can exit' sounds like the driver speaking; the answer is sitting inside those words.
explanation.definitionFit: A chicane is an artificial S-bend on a motor-racing circuit, placed to slow the cars and test drivers.

clue.text: Citizen of republic giving no backing to king

indicators.note: a word going backing runs backwards, from its end to its start

blocks.note: an old word for no
chess abbreviation

explanation.surface: A republican refuses to support the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about republicanism; the republic is the USA, whose people are nicknamed Yanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Yank is informal slang for an American, and the United States is a republic.

clue.text: Plays role differently, with new insertion for my part

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
N for new, inserted among the letters before they are mixed

explanation.surface: An actor takes a part in a new way, with a fresh scene added, speaking for themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With new insertion' tells you to add N to the letters before rearranging them.
explanation.definitionFit: Personally is used to mean speaking for oneself, as in stating one's own opinion.
